children: Apple will stage its most consequential product event in years on Wednesday, unveiling a truly new iPhone, a new chief executive as well as higher prices. It hopes consumers will concentrate on the first two.
The headline is expected to be the first foldable iPhone, an almost tabletlike device that fits comfortably in a pocket and allows people to use more than one app at a time.

Equally important will be the man introducing it. John Ternus took over as Apple's CEO last week, becoming Apple's third CEO since 1997, when Steve Jobs returned. Hopes are high that the longtime hardware engineering executive can spark a new wave of innovation and the foldable iPhone is the most significant Apple device in a decade.

The bad news for consumers is that Apple is expected to jack up iPhone prices. The cost of memory and storage chips inside the smartphone has quintupled since last fall, prompting Apple to raise prices across its device lineup to protect its profit margins.
The foldable iPhone will start at $2,200, estimates research firm IDC, while the Pro line of iPhones could jump in price by $200, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis.

Spread out over the term of a cellphone contract, or new installment plan, consumers might bite the bullet for the latest devices. Or they could take a breather after blowout sales of last year's iPhone 17 lineup.

The foldable and Pro model iPhones are expected to be the highlight, but Apple is also expected to release other devices, including new Apple Watch and Mac models, as well as updated AirPods and a new Apple TV box.

Notably two devices aren't expected to be on the menu: the base model iPhone, along with the second generation of the iPhone Air, which are expected next year. That means customers who want the latest model iPhone will have to pay up for the Pro models, potentially a clever strategy by Apple to push customers to more expensive models.

Foldable phones aren't new. Samsung released its first Galaxy Fold in 2019. Some companies even have tri-fold phones that have not one but two hinges. But the category has stalled, with shipments of foldables falling 15% in the first half of the year, says research firm IDC.

Apple's entry will be a shot in the arm for the category, IDC says, capturing 44% of the revenue generated by all foldable sales in 2026 even though it launches with just over three months to go in the year.

The hope is that Apple's foldable will be an advance over existing devices, particularly that its "crease" will be invisible. With Android foldables the crease where the display folds can be often noticeable, degrading the consumer experience.

As new CEO, Ternus will be the star of this year's show. At last year's event, while a mob of gadget reviewers rushed the displays of iPhone 17s, and swarmed Tim Cook, Ternus stood to the side, chatting quietly with other Apple executives and almost entirely ignored.

Ternus has been head of hardware engineering for Apple since 2021, leading the team that built the foldable iPhone. That team also incorporated Apple's highly rated chips in its Mac computers, one of its less appreciated but more consequential accomplishments of recent years.

It is no accident that Apple timed his transition so that, for his first product rollout, Ternus would introduce its biggest update to its most important product. One knock on Apple's Cook era has been that the company didn't release more innovative products. Though the foldable was developed on his watch, Apple is anxious to set a tone that a new innovative day has dawned at the company.
